description:
Constraint #6 (non-negotiable in AGENTS.md) says: 'Batch APIs where setup cost is non-trivial. Policy-adapter crates with subprocess overhead MUST expose batch APIs.' This crate's setup cost is one HTTP connection per fetch — high enough that batching becomes valuable when validating many chains.

Currently CachedHttpCrlFetcher / CachedHttpOcspFetcher are one-cert-at-a-time. A consumer validating a batch of 1000 chains hitting the same issuer's CRL gets 1000 cache lookups (good) but 1000 separate trait invocations (fine, but no opportunity to coalesce in-flight network fetches). The single-flight pattern — 'one cert's fetch in flight per (issuer, url) tuple, other concurrent waiters wait for that one fetch' — would be a significant additional win and is the canonical caching pattern for HTTP caches in this shape.

Scenario: 1000 concurrent OCSP checks against the same responder URL for the same issuer (e.g., 1000 client certs from the same root). With current code: cache-miss path runs concurrently 1000 times → 1000 HTTP POSTs → the responder hits rate-limit and starts dropping requests → most checks fail with RevocationFetchFailed.

Maintenance consequence: every consumer that hits this will either (a) build their own single-flight wrapper above CachedHttpCrlFetcher, fragmenting the cache abstraction, or (b) file an issue against this crate asking for single-flight. The principled answer is (b); the design space for the wrapper is documented enough that (a) shouldn't be needed.

Not blocking, but a 1.0-shape question: should the cache trait surface admit single-flight (e.g. a future inflight_get_or_fetch method), or stay strictly key→value and force single-flight into a separate composition layer?
title: Caller-side caching API design: callbacks are right, but consumers will reinvent batch wrappers
